The Slow Web Is Still Here

Notes on reading things properly.

Ada Quill
Mar 14, 2026

Every few months somebody announces that nobody reads anymore, and every few months I find another person who has quietly built a habit of reading long things slowly. The habit rarely looks impressive from outside. It looks like a list of links and an hour on a Sunday.1

The trouble is never a shortage of things worth reading. It is that the links arrive in a dozen inboxes at once, each with its own idea of what unread means, and none of them remembers what you finished.

Keeping what you finish

A reading list has two jobs. The first is to hold a link until you have time for it. The second, which almost every tool forgets, is to keep what you finished somewhere you can find it again when the half-remembered argument suddenly matters.

I call the second job the lighthouse problem. You remember that there was a lighthouse in the essay, and that it was a metaphor for something about attention, and nothing else. A decent archive lets you type lighthouse and get the essay back.2

Margin Notes is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts, consider becoming a subscriber.

So the test of a reading system is not how much it lets you save. It is whether, six months on, you can still find the one paragraph you need, and whether the queue in front of you is short enough to finish.

Start small: one place for links, one honest decision when you finish each of them. Keep it or let it go.

1

Sunday is not essential. A reader once wrote to say she does this on the ferry to work, twice a day, and has finished more essays than anyone I know.

2

The name is borrowed from the palimpsest of a seminar handout I have long since lost, which is rather the point.
